Photograph: Nikita Belov Finland Finland halts deportation of Russian family who ‘risked everything’ to oppose Ukraine invasion Mother and son Olga and Nikita Belov say they were facing jail and potential torture after asylum case was rejected Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent Mon 17 Aug 2026 10.04 EDT Last modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 10.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Russian family who were on the brink of being deported from Finland after repeatedly being denied asylum – despite the threat of arrest, imprisonment and torture for their pro-Ukrainian activism – have won a court appeal and will have their case reconsidered. Nikita Belov and his mother, Olga Belov, fled their homeland for Finland in 2022 after attracting the attention of Russian authorities – including a military summons, threatening messages and attempts to locate them – for expressing opposition to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine . They were due to be deported from Finland within weeks after the Finnish immigration service said they faced “no real risk” if they returned to Russia. In April they were temporarily detained by authorities pending deportation. The administrative court has quashed the decision, citing new evidence, including media coverage in Finnish, Russian and internationally, and referred the case back to the immigration service for fresh consideration. The Belovs’ case has gained political traction in neighbouring Norway. Last week politicians from Norway’s Green party tried to stage an intervention, proposing to the government that if the Belovs’ deportation went through, Norway should offer them asylum instead. The political activist and Putin critic Bill Browder , who is the head of the Global Magnitsky Justice Campaign, has said the case is “a defining test of Europe’s commitment to protecting those who have risked everything to oppose Putin’s war”. Nikita, 25, left his engineering job at a research institute in Moscow specialising in metallurgical technologies after finding out the work he was doing was connected to the Russian war effort. Since their arrival in Finland, Nikita and Olga, 55, a nurse anaesthetist, have been vocal supporters of Ukraine, sending humanitarian aid, including to the Ukrainian armed forces. Olga said the court’s decision marked the first positive news they had received in four years but that it was overshadowed by “constant uncertainty and fear of deportation”. She added: “My health has deteriorated over these four years, and we still have to wait for a final decision. This is very stressful, and nobody knows how long it will take. This experience has already left a lasting mark on our lives, and we will have to cope with the consequences. No matter what, I’d like to thank everybody who helps us, supports us, and literally saves us from death.” Nikita said: “Previously, when I imagined my reaction to a positive decision, I was sure it would be a very emotional moment. But actually, I felt nothing. It’s weird, but now it seems to me that I’m already mentally exhausted. We still have to wait for a final decision.” Their lawyer, who requested not to be named for security reasons, hopes they will be granted asylum soon. “The court has overturned the negative asylum decision as the clients have provided so much new evidence on them being profiled as being at risk of persecution,” they said. “The international attention and vast media coverage on the case and whether it puts them at risk has to be assessed accurately by the Finnish immigration service.” Browder, whose friend and lawyer Sergei Magnitsky died at the hands of Putin’s regime , said the latest decision was an “important victory for Nikita and Olga, but it should never have got this far”. He added: “Finland is on the frontline of defending Europe against Putin’s aggression. It would be completely perverse for it to send two people who have stood publicly against that aggression straight back into Putin’s hands. I hope the Finnish authorities will now grant Nikita and Olga the protection they deserve.” Antti Lehtinen, the director of the department for international protection at the Finnish immigration service, said he was unable to comment on individual cases, but added: “Only approximately 5% of all decisions are returned for reconsideration each year. The vast majority of these cases are due to the applicant presenting new information about their situation during the judicial proceedings. “The asylum decisions of the Finnish immigration service therefore correspond well with national legal practice and are also in line with the average decision-making practices of EU member states.” Explore more on these topics Finland Russia Ukraine Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Ukrainian drone attack on Russia kills at least six, says Moscow Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13 Blinded by War: documenting the aftermath of injury in Ukraine – photo essay Zelenskyy calls for more air defences as Russian attack on Kyiv kills at least 17 Ukrainian drone attacks on Black Sea resort and Crimea kill 11, Russia claims Russian missile destroys US firm’s Kyiv drone factory ‘Lenin was an enemy of humanity’: Why Kyiv wants to put Cossack chief statue in place of Soviet leader Rising Zelenskyy and falling Netanyahu cross paths in chaotic White House Burnham’s Ukraine gambit is a symbolic start for PM who wants to look inward Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/22/webs.text: Critical security flaws have been discovered in PHP, a widely used programming language that helps power around 70% of the world’s websites.Developers released emergency fixes on Wednesday, while cybersecurity authorities urged organisations to update affected systems immediately or take them offline until they could be secured.The warning prompted governments, companies and major online services in several countries to temporarily shut down websites and other systems as a precaution.The vulnerabilities were uncovered with the help of artificial intelligence. Security firm Calif identified one of the flaws in August during an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP, while Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities. OpenAI said its GPT-5.6 Sol model was used in the Calif research.The PHP security team rated both vulnerabilities 9.2 out of 10 for severity. Details were meant to remain confidential while developers prepared fixes, but information about the flaws emerged publicly before the planned release, intensifying the race to secure vulnerable systems.Security researchers initially reported little evidence of widespread exploitation before the vulnerabilities became public. However, attempted attacks have since been detected, increasing concern that unpatched systems could be targeted.Websites and services taken offlineThe Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia, said it deliberately took a number of supporting services offline while security updates were installed and warned users that some disruption could occur.Amazon Threat Intelligence also detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities, including activity before their public disclosure. Security researchers have since reported attempts to target vulnerable systems in the wild.Several European governments have also taken precautionary action.France’s Interior Ministry temporarily took prefecture websites offline while updates were applied, while Germany’s federal IT provider ITZBund shut down several government websites. German officials said the move was precautionary and that no security incidents had been identified.Government and public-service websites were also taken offline in countries including the Netherlands and Finland, as authorities worked to secure their systems.In the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre urged organisations running PHP to identify vulnerable systems, monitor them for suspicious activity and install security updates as soon as possible.
